title: The Pentecost novena
hook: the first novena, from Ascension to Pentecost

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was novena: nine days, one after another, practice in waiting. Your line was nine days. Did day two find its place? Day one thousand three hundred seventy-eight.

The friends of Jesus are walking back into Jerusalem from the hill called Olivet. A short walk. He's gone from their sight, in a way none of them can explain, and before he went he told them to wait. Not to preach yet, not to organize, not to scatter. Wait. So they climb the stairs to an upper room and do the one thing they've been asked to do. Nobody tells them how long it will take. Today we sit in that room with them.
screen: `BACK FROM OLIVET.` → `HE TOLD THEM TO WAIT.` → `UP THE STAIRS.`

segments.voice: Acts lists who's in the room, name by name: Peter and John, James and Andrew, and the rest. Then he adds more, in the Douay-Rheims: "All these were persevering with one mind in prayer with the women, and Mary the mother of Jesus, and with his brethren." So first: what tradition calls the first novena was not one person alone with a leaflet. It was a room full of people. Women, unnamed here. Jesus's family. His mother. Second, what they do there. Persevering, with one mind, in prayer. They're waiting for something they've been promised and can't produce themselves. Third, the end of the waiting. Acts two opens, in the Douay-Rheims: "And when the days of the Pentecost were accomplished, they were all together in one place." Pentecost was already a Jewish feast, the harvest feast Jews still keep as Shavuot, which is why the city is crowded with pilgrims. Then comes a sound from heaven like a mighty wind, tongues like fire, and the Spirit. Notice where it finds them: all together. Fourth, how the Church keeps it. Tradition counts the days from the Ascension to Pentecost as nine, and keeps them as a novena to the Holy Spirit. Pope Leo the Thirteenth, in a letter on the Holy Spirit, asked the whole Church to make that novena every year, and some parishes still mark it. One prayer used is just three words: Come, Holy Spirit. They open an old hymn and a well-worn prayer, and they say exactly what the upper room was doing. Waiting together is different from waiting alone. Someone else keeps the vigil when you nod off.
screen: `A ROOM FULL OF PEOPLE.` · `WITH ONE MIND, IN PRAYER.` · `ALL TOGETHER IN ONE PLACE.` · `COME, HOLY SPIRIT.` · then, large: `PERSEVERING WITH ONE MIND IN PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: come, Holy Spirit. Let the room around you go still. Bring to mind the people you're waiting alongside right now: a family waiting on news, coworkers waiting on a decision, a friend waiting to heal. In a way, you're in a room with them. If you pray, you can say the three words slowly on the out-breath: Come, Holy Spirit. Let them go out for the whole room, not only for yourself. If you don't pray, simply breathe out for those people, one by one. You might come back to this each day for a while. The bell holds the time.
The Pentecost novena. The days between the Ascension and Pentecost, kept as nine days of prayer to the Holy Spirit, in the pattern of the upper room. Today's word.

Your line: waiting together. Today, the next time you're stuck waiting, in a line, on hold, outside a door, notice who's waiting with you, and wish them well. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-eight.

howItsDone: Between the Ascension and Pentecost, some Catholics and parishes pray a novena to the Holy Spirit, often using the words come, Holy Spirit, or the hymns that begin with them.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Pentecost novena is a modern parish program.
what it means: the days from the Ascension to Pentecost, kept as nine days of prayer to the Spirit, in the pattern of the upper room.
what a scholar hears: Acts 1:14 puts Mary and the women in the room; Leo XIII, in his encyclical on the Holy Spirit, asked the whole Church to keep the novena.

notes: Leo XIII's Divinum Illud Munus asked that a novena to the Holy Spirit be made before Pentecost in parish churches (and later perpetually); the script says 'asked the whole Church to make that novena every year'. Confirm the section number and wording.
The count of nine days between the Ascension and Pentecost is attributed to tradition; Acts gives forty days of appearances (1:3) and does not count the waiting.
'Come, Holy Spirit' as the opening of an old hymn (Veni, Sancte Spiritus; cf. Veni, Creator Spiritus) and a common prayer; confirm phrasing.
Shavuot named briefly as the Jewish feast Pentecost was in Acts 2; confirm the neighbor mention is fair.
Day 1377 used Acts 1:4 (wait for the promise) and Matthew 6:7; this day uses Acts 1:14 and 2:1.
Douay-Rheims wording of Acts 1:14 and 2:1: confirm.

Editor pass: removed 'Acts records no sermon and no strategy meeting' (false: Acts 1:15–26 has Peter's speech and the choice of Matthias); 'Luke lists' now 'Acts lists'; 'the simplest prayer' superlative cut; Leviticus 23 cited for the harvest feast; varied the practice's settling line.
